fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. "…the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah." (2 Kings 24:17). The text says Babylon's king made him king. He even gave him a new name, Zedekiah.

Yes, friend. The text says Jehoiachin "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done." (2 Kings 24:9). His father was Jehoiakim, the king before him (2 Kings 24:6). Three months on the throne, and the writer still has that much to say about it.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jehoiachin "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father had done." (2 Kings 24:9). His father was Jehoiakim, the king before him (2 Kings 24:6). So the son did evil just as his father had, and this one doesn't need a second look.

I get the hope, friend, but the text never mentions a payment. It says the servants of Nebuchadnezzar marched up and "…the city came under siege." (2 Kings 24:10). That's what these verses give us. Jerusalem was under siege.

You got it, baker. Jehoiachin, his mother, his servants, his commanders and his officials "…all surrendered to the king of Babylon." (2 Kings 24:12). Nebuchadnezzar had come to the city himself (2 Kings 24:11). I think that took some nerve of its own, handing it all over with the king right there.

That would make a big scene, friend, but it isn't what the text says. Jehoiachin, his mother, his servants, his commanders and his officials "…all surrendered to the king of Babylon." (2 Kings 24:12). No charge out the gate is described in these verses. What we're told is that they surrendered.

Not this time, friend. The text says Nebuchadnezzar "…carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace…" (2 Kings 24:13). He didn't leave them where they were. He carried them off.
Right, baker. Nebuchadnezzar "…carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace…" (2 Kings 24:13). That covers the treasures in both places. None of them stayed put.

I wish it went that way, friend, but it doesn't. Nebuchadnezzar "…cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD." (2 Kings 24:13). Solomon was Israel's king long before this. What the text tells us is that they were cut into pieces.

Good guess, friend, but the text goes another way. Nebuchadnezzar "…cut into pieces all the gold articles that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the LORD." (2 Kings 24:13). Solomon was Israel's king long ago. The verse says the articles were cut into pieces, and it says nothing about handing them to anyone.

Close to something that sounds sensible, friend, but the text says "poorest." It reads, "Only the poorest people of the land remained." (2 Kings 24:14). The verse doesn't say a word about age. It says who was left: the poorest, after the commanders, mighty men, craftsmen and metalsmiths were taken.

That's right, baker. Nebuchadnezzar carried Jehoiachin to Babylon "…as well as the king’s mother, his wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land." (2 Kings 24:15). The wives are right there in the list. They were taken into exile too.

I see why you'd go there, friend, but the verse says otherwise. These men were "…all strong and fit for battle." (2 Kings 24:16). Trading doesn't come up in the verse at all. The word is battle, and these were seven thousand men of valor and a thousand craftsmen and metalsmiths.
